authors: Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Søren Leth-Petersen, Torben Heien Nielsen and Tore Olsen
title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark
summary: Uses the universe of Danish savings records to show that tax subsidies for retirement accounts mostly shift saving between accounts: each krone of subsidy raises total saving by about one øre. Automatic employer contributions, by contrast, raise total saving almost one for one, because roughly 85 percent of individuals are passive savers who do not re-optimise.
data: Income tax records with pension contributions

authors: Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, Camille Landais, Emmanuel Saez and Esben Schultz
title: Migration and Wage Effects of Taxing Top Earners: Evidence from the Foreigners' Tax Scheme in Denmark
summary: The 1991 preferential tax scheme for high-earning foreigners roughly doubled the number of highly paid foreigners in Denmark. The implied elasticity of migration with respect to the net-of-tax rate is above one, far larger than domestic labour supply elasticities, and the scheme generated modest wage spillovers.

authors: Katrine Jakobsen, Kristian Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven and Gabriel Zucman
title: Wealth Taxation and Wealth Accumulation: Theory and Evidence from Denmark
summary: Exploits the 1989 Danish wealth tax reform, which cut rates sharply for the wealthy, to estimate long-run effects of wealth taxes on wealth accumulation. Responses are sizable for the very wealthy (top one percent) and small for the moderately wealthy, with effects that keep growing over a decade.
data: Wealth tax records 1980–1996 (third-party reported assets and debt)

authors: Morten Bennedsen, Kasper Meisner Nielsen, Francisco Pérez-González and Daniel Wolfenzon
title: Inside the Family Firm: The Role of Families in Succession Decisions and Performance
summary: Uses the gender of a departing CEO's first-born child as an instrument for family succession in Danish firms. Family CEOs hurt performance: operating profitability falls by at least four percentage points relative to firms that hire outside CEOs, with the largest costs in fast-growing industries and large firms.
data: Family links from the population register (BEF)

authors: Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, Martin B. Knudsen, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Pedersen and Emmanuel Saez
title: Unwilling or Unable to Cheat? Evidence from a Tax Audit Experiment in Denmark
summary: A randomised field experiment with the Danish tax authority on about 40,000 taxpayers. Evasion is close to zero for third-party reported income but substantial for self-reported income, and audit threat letters raise reported self-reported income. Information, not morality, is what makes modern tax systems work.
data: Audit outcomes from the SKAT experiment

authors: Rasmus Lentz and Dale T. Mortensen
title: An Empirical Model of Growth Through Product Innovation
summary: Estimates a Schumpeterian model of firm growth through product innovation on a Danish firm panel. Reallocation of labour from less to more innovative firms accounts for roughly half of aggregate productivity growth, with the remainder coming from innovation within firms.
data: Firm panel from the Accounts Statistics (value added, employment, capital) 1992–1997

authors: Rasmus Lentz, Suphanit Piyapromdee and Jean-Marc Robin
title: The Anatomy of Sorting: Evidence from Danish Data
summary: Estimates a flexible model of worker and firm heterogeneity in wages and job mobility on Danish matched employer-employee data. Workers and firms sort positively, with sorting operating through both wages and non-wage amenities, and worker heterogeneity accounts for the bulk of wage dispersion.

authors: Jesper Bagger, François Fontaine, Fabien Postel-Vinay and Jean-Marc Robin
title: Tenure, Experience, Human Capital, and Wages: A Tractable Equilibrium Search Model of Wage Dynamics
summary: Builds and estimates an equilibrium search model with on-the-job search and human capital accumulation using Danish career histories. Human capital accumulation drives most early-career wage growth, while job-to-job mobility and employer competition explain the later part of wage profiles.
data: Matched employer-employee data (IDA) for male workers 1985–2003

authors: Jesper Bagger and Rasmus Lentz
title: An Empirical Model of Wage Dispersion with Sorting
summary: Estimates an equilibrium search model with endogenous search intensity and two-sided heterogeneity on Danish matched data. Finds positive assortative matching between worker and firm productivity, and quantifies how much of wage dispersion is due to sorting versus search frictions.

authors: David Hummels, Rasmus Jørgensen, Jakob Munch and Chong Xiang
title: The Wage Effects of Offshoring: Evidence from Danish Matched Worker-Firm Data
summary: Links product-level firm imports and exports to worker wages. Offshoring raises wages of high-skilled workers and lowers wages of low-skilled workers within job spells, while exporting raises wages for all. Tasks that are routine or easily offshored lose the most.
data: Firm-level foreign trade by product and country (UHDI)

authors: Søren Leth-Petersen
title: Intertemporal Consumption and Credit Constraints: Does Total Expenditure Respond to an Exogenous Shock to Credit?
summary: The 1992 reform that let Danish homeowners borrow against housing equity provides an exogenous credit shock. Total expenditure responded only modestly on average, with the response concentrated among young households with little liquid wealth, which indicates that credit constraints bind for a minority.
data: Consumption imputed from income minus change in wealth

authors: Thais Lærkholm Jensen and Niels Johannesen
title: The Consumption Effects of the 2007–2008 Financial Crisis: Evidence from Households in Denmark
summary: Customers of banks that were hit hard by the crisis cut consumption more than customers of healthier banks. The channel is reduced credit availability: exposed households borrowed less and spent less, which shows how bank distress transmits to the real economy through households.
data: Customer-bank links from tax reports on accounts and loans
Imputed consumption from income and wealth registers

authors: Steffen Andersen, John Y. Campbell, Kasper Meisner Nielsen and Tarun Ramadorai
title: Sources of Inaction in Household Finance: Evidence from the Danish Mortgage Market
summary: Many Danish households fail to refinance fixed-rate mortgages when it is clearly profitable. A model with inattention and psychological refinancing costs fits the data, and both frictions are stronger for households with less education, income and financial wealth.
data: Loan-level mortgage data from Danish mortgage banks
Income, wealth, education and demographics from registers

authors: Annette Alstadsæter, Niels Johannesen and Gabriel Zucman
title: Tax Evasion and Inequality
summary: Matches leaked offshore account data (HSBC Switzerland, Panama Papers) and tax amnesty records to Scandinavian wealth registers. Tax evasion rises steeply with wealth: the top 0.01 percent evade about a quarter of their taxes, which materially raises measured top wealth shares.
data: Danish, Norwegian and Swedish wealth and income tax records

authors: Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Family Health Behaviors
summary: A severe health shock to one family member, such as a heart attack or stroke, makes spouses and adult children raise their own preventive behaviour: more check-ups, more preventive medication and lifestyle changes. Responses are sharp, immediate and persistent, and they reflect updating about one's own risk.

authors: Anna Piil Damm and Christian Dustmann
title: Does Growing Up in a High Crime Neighborhood Affect Youth Criminal Behavior?
summary: Refugees arriving between 1986 and 1998 were allocated to municipalities quasi-randomly. Boys placed in neighbourhoods with a higher share of youth criminals were later more likely to be convicted, especially for violent crime, which identifies a causal neighbourhood effect on criminal behaviour.
data: Refugee placement records from the Danish Refugee Council

authors: Mikkel Aagaard Houmark, Victor Ronda and Michael Rosholm
title: The Nurture of Nature and the Nature of Nurture: How Genes and Investments Interact in the Formation of Skills
summary: Combines polygenic scores with register and survey measures of parental investment in a dynamic skill-formation model. Genetic endowments and investments interact: investments respond to children's endowments, and part of the measured genetic effect on skills runs through parental behaviour rather than biology alone.
data: Danish National Birth Cohort survey with genotype data

authors: Christian Dustmann, Kristine Vasiljeva and Anna Piil Damm
title: Refugee Migration and Electoral Outcomes
summary: Using the quasi-random refugee dispersal policy, refugee allocation raised vote shares for anti-immigration parties in rural municipalities and lowered them in the largest urban municipalities. Effects are strongest where refugees are few relative to natives and where crime rises after allocation.

authors: Kristoffer B. Hvidberg, Claus T. Kreiner and Stefanie Stantcheva
title: Social Positions and Fairness Views on Inequality
summary: Links a large survey to income registers to compare perceived and actual positions in the income distribution and within reference groups (co-workers, neighbours, schoolmates). People misperceive their rank, fairness views depend on the perceived gap to others, and showing people their true position changes their views.
data: Workplace, neighbourhood and education links (IDA, BEF, UDDA)
Custom survey matched on personal identifiers

authors: Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Children and Gender Inequality: Evidence from Denmark
summary: Event studies around the birth of the first child show mothers' earnings fall about 20 percent relative to fathers' in the long run, through hours, participation and wage rates. These child penalties now account for most of the remaining gender earnings gap and are transmitted across generations through mothers' own upbringing.

authors: Mette Foged and Giovanni Peri
title: Immigrants' Effect on Native Workers: New Analysis on Longitudinal Data
summary: Refugee-country immigration into Danish municipalities from 1991 to 2008 pushed less-educated native workers toward more complex, less manual occupations. Native wages and employment rose rather than fell, and effects were positive even for low-skilled natives who moved across firms.

authors: Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Family Labor Supply Responses to Severe Health Shocks: Evidence from Danish Administrative Records
summary: Compares households hit by a fatal versus a non-fatal health shock at the same time. After a spouse's death the surviving spouse raises labour supply to self-insure, while after a non-fatal shock spouses reduce labour supply to care for the patient. Children of the household adjust less.

authors: Henrik Jacobsen Kleven and Esben Anton Schultz
title: Estimating Taxable Income Responses Using Danish Tax Reforms
summary: Uses a series of Danish tax reforms between 1984 and 2005 and full-population tax records to estimate the elasticity of taxable income. Elasticities are small for labour income (around 0.05) and larger for capital income and for top earners, and they are larger for big reforms than small ones.

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen and Peer Ebbesen Skov
title: Tax Reforms and Intertemporal Shifting of Wage Income: Evidence from Danish Monthly Payroll Records
summary: The 2010 cut in the top marginal tax rate was announced in advance, and monthly payroll data show top earners shifting wage income from December 2009 into January 2010. Shifting is concentrated among managers and employees of small firms, and it inflates short-run elasticity estimates.

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, David Dreyer Lassen and Søren Leth-Petersen
title: Liquidity Constraint Tightness and Consumer Responses to Fiscal Stimulus Policy
summary: The 2009 payout of Special Pension savings worked as a fiscal stimulus. Measuring constraint tightness by the marginal interest rate households pay, the spending response is highest for households facing high marginal rates and otherwise small, which supports targeting stimulus at the credit constrained.
data: Tax records on interest payments and loans
Survey of spending responses linked to registers

authors: Helena Skyt Nielsen, Torben Sørensen and Christopher Taber
title: Estimating the Effect of Student Aid on College Enrollment: Evidence from a Government Grant Policy Reform
summary: A 1988 reform raised Danish student grants for students from higher-income families. Roughly 1,000 dollars of extra aid raised enrolment by about 1.35 percentage points, a response that is consistent with modest credit constraints rather than binding ones.

authors: Christian Dustmann, Rasmus Landersø and Lars Højsgaard Andersen
title: Refugee Benefit Cuts
summary: A 2002 reform cut welfare benefits for newly arrived refugees by roughly half. Employment rose modestly in the short run and then faded, while disposable income fell sharply. The cut raised crime among adults and harmed children's school enrolment and outcomes.

authors: Jeppe Druedahl and Alessandro Martinello
title: Long-Run Saving Dynamics: Evidence from Unexpected Inheritances
summary: Sudden parental deaths deliver unexpected inheritances. Heirs' wealth jumps and then declines over roughly a decade back toward its pre-inheritance path, which implies a moderate marginal propensity to consume out of wealth and informs the calibration of buffer-stock saving models.
data: Death register with cause of death

authors: Paul Bingley and Lorenzo Cappellari
title: Correlation of Brothers' Earnings and Intergenerational Transmission
summary: Decomposes the earnings correlation between Danish brothers into the part explained by fathers' earnings and the part due to other shared family and community factors. Intergenerational transmission accounts for a larger share of sibling similarity than simple father-son elasticities suggest, once permanent earnings and life-cycle bias are handled.
data: Income registers (IND) for fathers and sons

authors: N. Meltem Daysal, Marianne Simonsen, Mircea Trandafir and Sanni Breining
title: Spillover Effects of Early-Life Medical Interventions
summary: Extra medical treatment for very-low-birth-weight newborns, identified from a birth weight threshold, improves not only the treated infant but also the outcomes of older siblings, who do better in school. Family resources and parental time respond to the child's health.

authors: Martin Browning and Søren Leth-Petersen
title: Imputing Consumption from Income and Wealth Information
summary: Tests whether consumption can be imputed from register data as income minus the change in wealth, by comparing the imputation with expenditure survey responses for the same households. The imputation works well for most households but is noisy for those with housing transactions or large stock holdings.
data: Danish Expenditure Survey linked to registers

authors: Jakob Roland Munch, Michael Rosholm and Michael Svarer
title: Are Homeowners Really More Unemployed?
summary: Tests the Oswald hypothesis that home ownership raises unemployment. Danish homeowners are less geographically mobile, but they find local jobs faster, so their unemployment spells are shorter overall. Ownership does not raise aggregate unemployment.
data: Unemployment spells from IDA and benefit registers

authors: Rasmus Landersø, Helena Skyt Nielsen and Marianne Simonsen
title: School Starting Age and the Crime-Age Profile
summary: Children born just after the school start cut-off begin school almost a year later. Starting school older lowers crime at young ages, especially for boys, by shifting the crime-age profile rather than permanently reducing crime, consistent with an incapacitation and maturity channel.

authors: Simon Halphen Boserup, Wojciech Kopczuk and Claus Thustrup Kreiner
title: Born with a Silver Spoon? Danish Evidence on Wealth Inequality in Childhood
summary: Third-party reported wealth records of children show that wealth inequality is as high in childhood as among adults, with top shares driven by transfers from parents and grandparents. Wealth at age 18 predicts wealth in adulthood, and intergenerational wealth correlations are present from early ages.
data: Wealth registers (FORM) for children and parents

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen and Louise Charlotte Willerslev-Olsen
title: Financial Trouble Across Generations: Evidence from the Universe of Personal Loans in Denmark
summary: Loan-level records on all personal loans show strong intergenerational persistence in financial trouble: children of parents who default are far more likely to default themselves, and the correlation is present already in early adulthood and is not explained by income or education.
data: Universe of personal loans reported to the tax authority (loan-level, with default status)

authors: Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Tore Olsen and Luigi Pistaferri
title: Adjustment Costs, Firm Responses, and Micro vs. Macro Labor Supply Elasticities: Evidence from Danish Tax Records
summary: Uses bunching at kinks in the Danish tax schedule to show that observed earnings responses are shaped by search costs and by firms coordinating hours around tax thresholds. Once adjustment frictions are accounted for, the structural labour supply elasticity is around 0.3, far above the small elasticities from individual-level micro studies, which helps reconcile micro and macro estimates.

authors: Sharon Traiberman
title: Occupations and Import Competition: Evidence from Denmark
summary: Estimates a dynamic occupational choice model on Danish worker histories in which workers accumulate occupation-specific human capital that is lost when they switch. Occupations explain 57 percent of the dispersion in worker outcomes from trade, sectors only 16 percent, and rising import competition from 1995 to 2005 lowered lifetime earnings for about 5 percent of workers.
data: Matched employer-employee data (IDA) with occupation codes 1995–2005

authors: Thomas Epper, Ernst Fehr, Helga Fehr-Duda, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, David Dreyer Lassen, Søren Leth-Petersen and Gregers Nytoft Rasmussen
title: Time Discounting and Wealth Inequality
summary: Links incentivised time-discounting experiments to the wealth positions of a large sample of middle-aged Danes in the registers. Patient individuals sit markedly higher in the wealth distribution, and the association survives controls for education, income profiles, school grades, initial and parental wealth, credit constraints and risk preferences, which points to saving behaviour as the channel.
data: Incentivised online experiment linked on PNR

authors: Anders Humlum, Jakob R. Munch and Pernille Plato
title: Changing Tracks: Human Capital Investment after Loss of Ability
summary: Uses quasi-random work accidents in Danish administrative data to show that injured workers enrol in bachelor's programmes that build on their previous training. Exploiting differences in how stackable degrees are, higher education moves injured workers from disability benefits into full-time jobs paying 25 percent more than before injury, and reskilling subsidies pay for themselves four times over.
data: Work accident records linked to the National Patient Register
Income, employment and disability benefit registers (IND, IDA, DREAM)

authors: Henrik Kleven, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Kristian Larsen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Micro versus Macro Labor Supply Elasticities: The Role of Dynamic Returns to Effort
summary: Builds a model in which effort today raises earnings tomorrow, so responses to taxes are delayed and mediated by job switches. Danish administrative data confirm the model's life-cycle predictions for earnings and hours, and a quasi-experimental design based on job switchers finds a long-run earnings elasticity around 0.5, against a short-run elasticity of about 0.2.
data: Hours and job spells from payroll data (BFL) and IDA

authors: N. Meltem Daysal, Hui Ding, Maya Rossin-Slater and Hannes Schwandt
title: Germs in the Family: The Short- and Long-Term Consequences of Intrahousehold Disease Spread
summary: Shows that infant younger siblings are hospitalised for respiratory conditions two to three times as often as their older siblings were, because preschool-aged children bring disease home. Combining birth order with local variation in respiratory disease prevalence, early-life exposure lowers younger siblings' later earnings and education and worsens chronic respiratory and mental health.
data: Medical Birth Register and family links (MFR, BEF)

authors: Thomas H. Jørgensen, Katrine Jakobsen and Hamish Low
title: Fertility and Family Labor Supply
summary: Uses the 2009 Danish tax reform to show that higher net-of-tax wages for women reduce fertility while higher wages for men raise it. A life-cycle model of couples choosing the timing and number of children, estimated on register data, implies that allowing fertility to adjust raises women's labour supply responsiveness substantially and that human capital depreciation around births drives much of the long-run gender wage gap.
data: Income tax records and tax reform variation

authors: Christian Dustmann and Rasmus Landersø
title: Child's Gender, Young Fathers' Crime, and Spillover Effects in Criminal Behavior
summary: Uses the gender of a first-born child as a natural experiment for young fathers in Denmark. Having a son rather than a daughter lowers the father's subsequent criminal behaviour, and the reduction spills over to the father's peers and later to the child, which identifies both a direct parenting response and network effects in crime.

authors: Christopher Taber and Rune Vejlin
title: Estimation of a Roy/Search/Compensating Differential Model of the Labor Market
summary: Combines a Roy model, search frictions, compensating differentials and on-the-job human capital accumulation in one framework, establishes what is non-parametrically identified, and estimates it on Danish matched data. Pre-market skills account for most wage variation, while preferences for non-wage job attributes and search frictions matter greatly for turnover and for which jobs workers choose.

authors: Benjamin U. Friedrich and Martin B. Hackmann
title: The Returns to Nursing: Evidence from a Parental-Leave Program
summary: A Danish parental-leave programme offering up to a year off per child aged 0 to 8 induced a nurse shortage that hospitals and nursing homes could not replace. Nurse employment fell by 15 percent in hospitals and 10 percent in nursing homes, 30-day readmissions of heart attack patients rose, and nursing home mortality increased sharply.
data: Matched employer-employee data (IDA) for health workers

authors: Andrew Caplin, Victoria Gregory, Eungik Lee, Søren Leth-Petersen and Johan Sæverud
title: Subjective Earnings Risk
summary: Introduces a survey instrument for earnings risk that allows for quitting and being fired, fielded to Danish workers and linked to their register earnings histories. Job transitions drive subjective risk, which is many times smaller than traditional register-based estimates even after conditioning on demographics and job history, and helps explain why many hold few liquid assets.

authors: Dmitry Taubinsky, Luigi Butera, Matteo Saccarola and Chen Lian
title: Beliefs About the Economy Are Excessively Sensitive to Household-Level Shocks: Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
summary: Links Statistics Denmark's consumer expectations survey to the registers to show that people's inflation forecasts and backcasts move strongly, and negatively, with their own recent and expected income changes, far more than actual inflation does. The pattern departs from Bayesian rational expectations and is consistent with affect-cued recall, where bad personal events cue pessimistic recollections.
data: Consumer expectations survey linked on PNR

authors: Asger Lau Andersen, Kilian Huber, Niels Johannesen, Ludwig Straub and Emil Toft Vestergaard
title: Disaggregated Economic Accounts
summary: Builds a system of national accounts broken down into bilateral money flows between region-by-industry consumer cells, producer cells, the government and the rest of the world, and implements it for Denmark using bank transaction data and registers. Spending is locally and urban biased, and fiscal transfers raise GDP more when targeted at cells whose spending reaches cells with high unemployment.
data: Geocoded transaction data from Danske Bank
Firm accounts and VAT data (FIRE, VNDS)

authors: Ole Agersnap, Amalie Sofie Jensen and Henrik Kleven
title: The Welfare Magnet Hypothesis: Evidence from an Immigrant Welfare Scheme in Denmark
summary: The 2002 cut in benefits for non-EU immigrants, its repeal and its reintroduction provide repeated quasi-experiments on the welfare magnet hypothesis. The cut reduced net immigration by about 5,000 people a year and the repeal reversed it almost exactly, implying a migration elasticity with respect to benefits of 1.3.

authors: Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Does Biology Drive Child Penalties? Evidence from Biological and Adoptive Families
summary: Compares event-study child penalties for biological and adoptive mothers using almost 40 years of Danish adoption data. Short-run penalties are slightly larger for biological mothers, but long-run penalties are virtually identical, so biology is not a key driver of child-related gender gaps.

authors: Asger Lau Andersen, Niels Johannesen and Adam Sheridan
title: Dynamic Spending Responses to Wealth Shocks: Evidence from Quasi Lotteries on the Stock Market
summary: Uses lottery-like variation in stock market gains across investors with similar portfolios, observed in granular bank data, to trace spending responses. Responses are immediate and persistent, cumulating to a marginal propensity to consume of 4.4 percent over one year and 16 percent over three, consistent with the permanent income hypothesis with some inattention.
data: Account-level spending and stock portfolios from Danske Bank

authors: Niels Johannesen, Johan Sæverud and Emmanuel Saez
title: Taxing the Wealth of the Poor: Evidence from the Danish Old-Age Support Asset Test
summary: The asset test for Danish old-age support creates diffuse but large excess mass in liquid assets just below the threshold among the eligible, relative to comparable ineligible groups. Cohort analysis suggests the test reduces liquid assets by about 20 percent near the threshold, and high-frequency bank data show the responses are permanent rather than timed around the test date.

authors: Itzik Fadlon, Astrid Sophie Fugleholm and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Survivors' Mental Health and the Protective Role of Income Stability
summary: Documents the immediate, large and lingering rise in mental health medication after a spouse's death across the universe of Danish households. A large share of the spike is explained by the income loss the death imposes, so safety-net liquidity protects survivors' mental health.

authors: Anders Humlum and Pernille Plato
title: Reskilling and Resilience
summary: Studies how retraining shapes workers' resilience to labour market shocks in Danish administrative data, extending the authors' work on human capital investment after injury to the question of which workers reskill and how reskilling protects earnings when jobs disappear.
data: Employment and earnings registers (IDA, BFL, IND)

authors: Hale Utar
title: When the Floodgates Open: Northern Firms' Response to Removal of Trade Quotas on Chinese Goods
summary: The dismantling of Multi-Fibre Arrangement quotas on Chinese textiles at WTO accession exposed Danish textile firms to low-wage competition. Within firms, employment, value added and intangible assets fell and the workforce shifted toward skilled workers, while firms refocused away from products where China's advantage grew.

authors: Itzik Fadlon, Jessica Laird and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Do Employer Pension Contributions Reflect Employee Preferences? Evidence from a Retirement Savings Reform in Denmark
summary: A reform that cut the subsidy to capital pension accounts for top-bracket workers led employers to reduce contributions to those accounts immediately, by more the larger the share of affected employees, and to shift the money to annuity accounts. Employer contributions track employees' savings preferences.
data: Pension contribution records from tax data

authors: Jonas Hjort, Mikkel Sølvsten and Miriam Wüst
title: Universal Investment in Infants and Long-Run Health: Evidence from Denmark's 1937 Home Visiting Program
summary: Uses the staggered municipal roll-out of the 1937 universal infant home visiting programme and follows treated cohorts into middle age in the registers. Treated individuals have higher survival between ages 45 and 64, fewer hospital nights and less cardiovascular disease, consistent with early nutrition and disease environment programming adult health.

authors: Maya Rossin-Slater and Miriam Wüst
title: What Is the Added Value of Preschool for Poor Children? Long-Term and Intergenerational Impacts and Interactions with an Infant Health Intervention
summary: Access to preschool targeted at low-income children between 1933 and 1960 raised adult education, earnings and survival past 65, and the children of exposed women obtained more education by 25. Exposure to the nurse home visiting programme in infancy reduces preschool's added value, so the two programmes are partial substitutes.

authors: Anne Sofie Tegner Anker, Jennifer L. Doleac and Rasmus Landersø
title: The Effects of DNA Databases on the Deterrence and Detection of Offenders
summary: A large expansion of Denmark's DNA database cut recidivism within a year by up to 42 percent and raised the chance that re-offenders are caught, implying that a 1 percent higher detection probability lowers crime by more than 2 percent. Registered offenders also became more likely to work, study and live in stable families.

authors: Asger Lau Andersen, Amalie Sofie Jensen, Niels Johannesen, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen and Adam Sheridan
title: How Do Households Respond to Job Loss? Lessons from Multiple High-Frequency Datasets
summary: Combines bank transaction data with government registers to measure every margin of self-insurance after job loss. Over two years households cut spending by 30 percent of the income loss and cover about half of it by running down liquid balances; spousal labour supply, private transfers, home equity extraction and consumer credit contribute less.
data: Account-level spending, balances and loans from Danske Bank

authors: Christian Dustmann, Rasmus Landersø and Lars Højsgaard Andersen
title: Unintended Consequences of Welfare Cuts on Children and Adolescents
summary: The 2002 benefit cut for newly arrived refugees reduced family disposable income by 30 percent over five years. Children exposed at preschool or school age obtained lower grades, less education and lower adult earnings, and teenagers at exposure saw large increases in convictions for violent and property crime.
data: Residence permit dates and benefit registers (DREAM)

authors: Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Alan Manning
title: Background Matters, but Not Whether Parents Are Immigrants: Outcomes of Children Born in Denmark
summary: Children born in Denmark to immigrant parents have lower earnings, more unemployment, less education, more transfers and more convictions than children of Danish-born parents. Conditional on parental socioeconomic characteristics, however, they do as well or slightly better, so the gaps reflect deprived backgrounds rather than immigrant parentage.
data: Population register with origin and parent links (BEF)
Income, education, benefit and crime registers

authors: Jonathan Gruber, Amalie Sofie Jensen and Henrik Kleven
title: Do People Respond to the Mortgage Interest Deduction? Quasi-Experimental Evidence from Denmark
summary: A major reform that scaled back the mortgage interest deduction for middle- and high-income households had a precisely estimated zero effect on home ownership. It did reduce the size and price of houses bought, lowered household indebtedness and pushed down equilibrium house prices.
data: Income tax records with interest deductions

authors: Esteban García-Miralles and Jonathan M. Leganza
title: Public Pensions and Private Savings
summary: A Danish reform raising the social security eligibility age, studied with a regression discontinuity in administrative data, increased contributions to personal and employer pension accounts when later eligibility kept people working longer. Inertia in previous savings behaviour and firms' default contribution rates are the key mechanisms.

authors: N. Meltem Daysal, William N. Evans, Mikkel Hasse Pedersen and Mircea Trandafir
title: Do Medical Treatments Work for Work? Evidence from Breast Cancer Patients
summary: A Danish guideline change shifted which breast cancer patients received radiation therapy, giving quasi-experimental variation in treatment. Radiotherapy reproduces the survival gains found in trials and has economic returns: ten years after diagnosis it raises employment by 37 percent and earnings by 45 percent, undoing most of the post-diagnosis employment drop.

authors: Tobias Renkin and Gabriel Züllig
title: Credit Supply Shocks and Prices: Evidence from Danish Firms
summary: Combines loan-level data on Danish firm–bank relationships with survey producer prices and export unit values. Firms whose banks were exposed to the global financial crisis saw loans fall and rates rise, and they raised output prices by 3 to 5 percent to generate cash, with smaller increases where demand is more elastic.
data: Firm–bank loan data from the central bank
Export unit values from foreign trade data (UHDI)

authors: Hale Utar
title: Workers beneath the Floodgates: Low-Wage Import Competition and Workers' Adjustment
summary: Follows Danish textile and clothing workers for a decade after the removal of quotas on Chinese imports, using within-industry and within-occupation differences in exposure. Earnings and employment fall persistently, job instability in services is the main adjustment friction, and workers with manufacturing-specific education rebuild human capital through further schooling.

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Daniel Reck and Peer Ebbesen Skov
title: Do Lower Minimum Wages for Young Workers Raise Their Employment? Evidence from a Danish Discontinuity
summary: Danish minimum wages jump by 40 percent at age 18. Monthly payroll records for the whole population show employment falling by 33 percent and hours by 45 percent at the discontinuity, leaving total wage payments almost unchanged, with an implied employment elasticity between 0.6 and 1.1.
data: Monthly payroll records (BFL) with hours and wages
Population register (BEF) for exact birth dates

authors: Gordon B. Dahl, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Torben Heien Nielsen and Benjamin Ly Serena
title: Understanding the Rise in Life Expectancy Inequality
summary: Decomposes widening life expectancy gaps between rich and poor into changes in age-specific mortality and differences in survivability to each age. Lower survivability of the poor explains the entire rise in Danish life expectancy inequality; cardiovascular gains helped everyone, but lifestyle-related survivability diverged.

authors: Mette Foged, Linea Hasager, Giovanni Peri, Jacob Nielsen Arendt and Iben Bolvig
title: Language Training and Refugees' Integration
summary: A 1999 reform improved language training for newly recognised refugees. A regression discontinuity around the cut-off date shows a permanent, positive effect on earnings that emerges after classes are completed, together with more schooling and a higher probability of working in complex jobs.

authors: Olivier B. Bargain and Anders B. Jonassen
title: New Evidence on Welfare's Disincentive for the Youth Using Administrative Panel Data
summary: Maximum social assistance for childless unmarried Danes rose by 55 percent at age 25 between 2000 and 2006. Only the low-skilled respond: employment falls by 2 to 3 percent and benefit take-up rises by 10 to 14 percent, two thirds through moves from work to welfare, and crime shows no discontinuity.

authors: Onur Altındağ, Jane Greve and Erdal Tekin
title: Public Health Policy at Scale: Impact of a Government-Sponsored Information Campaign on Infant Mortality in Denmark
summary: A nationwide campaign against sudden infant death syndrome, delivered mainly through universal nurse home visits, cut infant mortality by 17 percent in a regression discontinuity on population birth data. Effects were 11 to 14 times larger for low-birthweight and preterm infants and concentrated among low-SES families.

authors: Ida Lykke Kristiansen and Sophie Yanying Sheng
title: The Physician-Patient Match and Health Inequality
summary: Measures general practitioners' childhood socioeconomic status from their parents' education in the registers. Low-SES patients matched to a GP of similar background have substantially lower mortality, while high-SES patients are unaffected, cutting the SES mortality gradient by a quarter through more intensive care, better detection of chronic conditions and better adherence.
data: GP–patient assignment and primary care contacts
Physician family background from BEF and UDDA

authors: Anne Toft Hansen, Jonas Cuzulan Hirani and Miriam Wüst
title: Depressed Peers in Early Parenthood
summary: Municipal nurses assign new mothers to postnatal peer groups essentially arbitrarily conditional on a few characteristics. Exposure to a depressed peer raises a mother's own mental health care use by 11 percent two years after birth and worsens her self-reported mental health and labour market outcomes.
data: Postnatal care group assignments from municipal nurse records

authors: Magnus T. Buus, Jakob R. Munch, Joel Rodrigue and Georg Schaur
title: Do Export Support Programs Affect Prices, Quality, Markups, and Marginal Costs? Evidence From a Natural Policy Experiment
summary: Uses a quasi-natural experiment in the Danish Trade Council's export support to firms. Support raises firm-level exports within destination markets but leaves prices, quality, markups and marginal costs unchanged, consistent with firms growing abroad by shifting demand rather than changing products.
data: Firm-level exports by product and destination (UHDI)

authors: Karsten Albæk and Bent E. Sørensen
title: Worker Flows and Job Flows in Danish Manufacturing, 1980–91
summary: One of the first uses of the IDA matched employer-employee data to measure job creation, job destruction and worker flows across Danish manufacturing plants. Worker turnover far exceeds job reallocation, and both are large and persistent at the plant level.

authors: Lars Pico Geerdsen
title: Is there a Threat Effect of Labour Market Programmes? A Study of ALMP in the Danish UI System
summary: Exploits the timing rules for compulsory activation in the Danish unemployment insurance system to test whether the prospect of being activated speeds up exit from unemployment. Exit rates rise markedly as the activation deadline approaches, which identifies a sizeable threat effect of active labour market programmes.

authors: Eskil Heinesen
title: Estimating Class-size Effects using Within-school Variation in Subject-specific Classes
summary: Uses within-school variation over time in the size of French classes, which Danish seventh graders choose between French and German, as quasi-random variation in class size. Larger classes lower French exam marks, especially for weaker students and boys, and marks in subjects taught in the regular class serve as a check on selection.
data: Parental background from BEF and UDDA

authors: Martin Browning, Mette Gørtz and Søren Leth-Petersen
title: Housing Wealth and Consumption: A Micro Panel Study
summary: Uses register-based imputed consumption and house price changes over the 1987 to 1996 boom and bust to test whether housing wealth drives spending. For most households consumption does not respond to unanticipated house price changes; the response is confined to young households, consistent with a collateral rather than a wealth effect.
data: Income and wealth tax records with property values
Consumption imputed from income and wealth changes

authors: Jesper Bagger, Javier A. Birchenall, Hani Mansour and Sergio Urzúa
title: Education, Birth Order and Family Size
summary: Develops a model of parental investment with birth order preferences and human capital cost differences that delivers a generalised quantity–quality trade-off. Danish administrative data confirm its predictions: at any given parity, children in smaller families have more education, and the average child's education falls with family size even after accounting for birth order.

authors: Jennifer L. Baker, Lise G. Bjerregaard, Christian M. Dahl, Torben S. D. Johansen, Emil N. Sørensen and Miriam Wüst
title: Universal Investments in Toddler Health: Learning from a Large Government Trial
summary: A 1960s Copenhagen government trial of preventive health care for toddlers, documented from handwritten nurse records and linked to the registers, improved a good adult health index by five percent of a standard deviation. Gains are largest for initially disadvantaged children and girls and fade for later cohorts as the counterfactual policy environment improved.
data: Digitised nurse records from the trial

authors: Sarah Sander
title: Universal Daycare and Mothers' Working Lifetime
summary: Exploits the roll-out of daycare centres across Danish municipalities to follow mothers over their working lives. Daycare availability raises participation, hours and earnings sixteen years after the first birth, with effects driven by low-educated mothers and mediated partly through fertility and separation.

authors: Petter Lundborg, Erik Plug and Astrid Würtz Rasmussen
title: Can Women Have Children and a Career? IV Evidence from IVF Treatments
summary: Uses success in in vitro fertilisation treatment among childless Danish women as an instrument for having children, since IVF success is unrelated to labour market history. Children lower women's earnings substantially and persistently, mostly through hourly earnings rather than hours, and the effect is much larger for the first child than for later ones.
data: IVF treatment records from the Danish fertility clinics register

authors: Steffen Andersen, Cristian Badarinza, Lu Liu, Julie Marx and Tarun Ramadorai
title: Reference Dependence in the Housing Market
summary: Combines Danish housing listings and transactions with register data on owners to estimate a structural model of listing and sale decisions with loss aversion and financial constraints. Households derive utility from gains over the original purchase price and weigh losses about 2.5 times more than gains, which helps explain the co-movement of house prices and turnover.
data: Household wealth and mortgage data from registers (FORM)

authors: Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Ning Zhang
title: Effects of Parental Death on Labor Market Outcomes
summary: Uses sudden first parental deaths and matched controls in Danish administrative data. Earnings fall by about 2 percent for men and 3 percent for women, mental health worsens for both, and women with young children lose the most, around 4 percent, consistent with the loss of informal childcare from grandparents.

authors: Katrine Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven, Jonas Kolsrud, Camille Landais and Mathilde Muñoz
title: Taxing Top Wealth: Migration Responses and Their Aggregate Economic Implications
summary: Uses Danish and Swedish administrative data to estimate how the wealthy migrate in response to wealth taxes. A one percentage point higher top wealth tax rate reduces the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent and hurts the businesses of departing owners, but the aggregate effects on employment, investment and value added are small.

authors: Kenneth Gillingham, Fedor Iskhakov, Anders Munk-Nielsen, John Rust and Bertel Schjerning
title: Equilibrium Trade in Automobiles
summary: Develops and estimates a dynamic equilibrium model of the market for new and used cars with heterogeneous households on the universe of Danish car ownership records, which record every vehicle's owner, age and scrappage. The model is used to evaluate Denmark's very high registration taxes and fuel taxes, showing how tax changes propagate through used-car prices and the age distribution of the fleet.
data: Danish motor vehicle register (ownership, transactions, scrappage)
Household income and demographics from registers

authors: Giacomo De Giorgi, Anders Frederiksen and Luigi Pistaferri
title: Consumption Network Effects
summary: Measures household consumption from Danish tax records on income and assets and defines peer groups by workplace using matched employer-employee data. Instrumenting peers' consumption with shocks to their own non-overlapping networks and firms, the paper finds sizeable consumption spillovers that can generate macro multipliers, operating through both intertemporal and intratemporal channels.
data: Imputed consumption from income and wealth registers (IND, FORM)
Matched employer-employee data (IDA) for co-worker networks

authors: Wolfgang Keller and Hale Utar
title: Globalization, Gender, and the Family
summary: Men and women hit by the same import shock from China adjust differently. Women in their late thirties who are displaced respond by having a child, especially high earners and those who would need to retrain, so a gender-neutral trade shock produces a long-run gender gap through the biological clock.

authors: Petter Lundborg, Erik Plug and Astrid Würtz Rasmussen
title: On the Family Origins of Human Capital Formation: Evidence from Donor Children
summary: Uses Danish children conceived through sperm and egg donation to separate nurture from genetic transmission, since donors are not selected on parental traits. Only mothers' education matters once genes are removed: fathers' schooling has no effect on children's test scores, while mothers' schooling raises reading scores as much as among non-donor children.

authors: Hanno Foerster
title: Untying the Knot: How Child Support and Alimony Affect Couples' Dynamic Decisions and Welfare
summary: Estimates a dynamic model of family labour supply, home production, saving and divorce on Danish register and survey data to study post-marital maintenance payments. Alimony carries larger labour supply disincentives and insures consumption less efficiently than child support, so welfare rises when child support is increased and alimony reduced.
data: Income, employment and marital status registers
Child support and alimony payment records

authors: Ufuk Akcigit, Jeremy Pearce and Marta Prato
title: Tapping into Talent: Coupling Education and Innovation Policies for Economic Growth
summary: Builds an endogenous growth model with heterogeneous talent, financial resources and career choice, and links it to Danish micro data on who obtains a PhD and who becomes an inventor. R&D subsidies work better when combined with higher education subsidies that let talented but poor youth pursue research, and education policy matters most in unequal societies.
data: Inventor records from patent data linked to PNR

authors: Steffen Altmann, Anita M. Glenny, Robert Mahlstedt and Alexander Sebald
title: The Direct and Indirect Effects of Online Job Search Advice
summary: A large two-stage randomised experiment on the Danish public employment service's online platform gave job seekers vacancy information and occupational recommendations, with treatment intensity varying by region. Advice raises employment and earnings when few job seekers receive it, but the gains vanish at high intensity because treated job seekers crowd into the same occupations.
data: Jobnet platform data and experimental assignment

authors: Andrey Stoyanov and Nikolay Zubanov
title: Productivity Spillovers Across Firms through Worker Mobility
summary: Tracks firm-to-firm worker moves in Danish manufacturing. Firms that hire workers from more productive firms see productivity gains of about 0.35 percent a year for an average firm, rising with the education, tenure and skill of the new hires and persisting for several years, consistent with knowledge spillovers carried by workers.

authors: Steffen Andersen, Elin Colmsjö, Gianpaolo Parise and Kim Peijnenburg
title: Breaking Bad: How Health Shocks Prompt Crime
summary: Uses plausibly exogenous timing of cancer diagnoses in Danish registers to show that a health shock raises the probability of committing a crime, both first offences and re-offences, persistently. Patients replace lost legal income with illegal income and face a lower expected cost of punishment because of reduced survival, and welfare programmes that cushion the income loss dampen the effect.
data: Cancer registry and National Patient Register

authors: Edmund Crawley and Andreas Kuchler
title: Consumption Heterogeneity: Micro Drivers and Macro Implications
summary: Estimates marginal propensities to consume across Danish households with a method that corrects biases in earlier register-based estimates. Liquid wealth is the dominant predictor of MPCs, and the estimated heterogeneity is used to quantify monetary policy transmission in Denmark and the United States.
data: Imputed consumption from income and wealth registers (IND, FORM)

authors: Jakob Munch and Georg Schaur
title: The Effect of Export Promotion on Firm-Level Performance
summary: Evaluates the Danish Trade Council's export promotion services, separating firms that sought help from firms the council approached on observables. Promotion raises sales, value added, employment and value added per worker, and for small firms the gain in value added is roughly three times the direct cost.

authors: Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen and Mikkel Høst Gandil
title: Attendance Boundary Policies and the Limits to Combating School Segregation
summary: Uses address-level data on the universe of Danish children and changes in school attendance boundaries over time. Households defy reassignment to schools with lower socioeconomic status, resourceful households most of all, so redrawing boundaries toward highly disadvantaged schools barely changes those schools' composition.
data: Address histories and school enrolment registers

authors: Jonas Fluchtmann, Anita M. Glenny, Nikolaj A. Harmon and Jonas Maibom
title: The Gender Application Gap: Do Men and Women Apply for the Same Jobs?
summary: Uses administrative records of the job applications made by every Danish unemployment insurance recipient. Men and women apply to very different job types even when observationally similar, and these differences in applications account for more than 70 percent of the residual gender wage gap.
data: Job application logs from the public employment service (Jobnet)
Unemployment insurance and wage registers (DREAM, BFL)

authors: Marianne Simonsen and Lars Skipper
title: Healthy at Work? Evidence from a Social Experimental Evaluation of a Firm-Based Wellness Program
summary: A large social experiment across worksites, followed for up to twelve years in the registers, evaluates an employer-sponsored health programme. Employees at treated worksites see fewer GP visits and buy fewer prescription drugs for up to seven years, with no change in hospitalisations, absence or turnover and some spillovers within the family.

authors: William W. Olney and Dario Pozzoli
title: The Impact of Immigration on Firm-Level Offshoring
summary: Uses the Danish refugee dispersal policy as a natural experiment and matched data on all firms and workers from 1995 to 2011. An exogenous inflow of immigrants into a municipality reduces firm-level offshoring on both margins, while immigrants' ties to their origin countries raise offshoring to those particular countries.

authors: Benjamin U. Friedrich
title: Trade Shocks, Firm Hierarchies, and Wage Inequality
summary: Shows that trade shocks change within-firm wage inequality by changing firm hierarchies, using both firm-level foreign demand shocks and the Muslim boycott of Danish exports after the 2006 cartoon crisis. Adding a hierarchy layer widens pay gaps throughout the firm, and delayering after the boycott compresses wages through cuts, demotions and turnover.
data: Matched employer-employee data with occupation hierarchies (IDA)

authors: Henrik Yde Andersen, Stine Ludvig Bech and Alessia De Stefani
title: Spending Response to a Predictable Increase in Mortgage Repayments: Evidence from Expiring Interest-Only Loans
summary: Matches the universe of Danish mortgages to borrower registers and studies the fully anticipated start of amortisation on interest-only loans. When instalments rise by 9 percent of income, consumption falls by 3 percent of income and stays down, with the failure to smooth concentrated among highly leveraged borrowers likely to be refused a new interest-only loan.
data: Loan-level mortgage data from mortgage banks
Imputed consumption from income and wealth registers

authors: Gustaf Bruze, Alexander Kjær Hilsløv and Jonas Maibom
title: The Long-Run Effects of Individual Debt Relief
summary: Links court records on the Danish debt relief programme to the registers and uses quasi-random assignment of applicants to court trustees with different admission rates. Debt relief raises earned income, employment, assets, home ownership and wealth for more than 25 years, with the move into employment accounting for two thirds of the income gain.
data: Court records on debt relief applications
Income, employment and wealth registers (IND, IDA, FORM)

authors: David Hummels, Jakob R. Munch and Chong Xiang
title: No Pain, No Gain: Work Demand, Work Effort, and Worker Health
summary: Links Danish worker-firm data to hospital and prescription records to study how rising workload affects health. Increases in firm sales lead workers to log longer hours and raise the probability of stress, depression, heart disease and stroke, most for older and already strained workers; the welfare loss from sickness offsets nearly a quarter of the earnings gain.
data: Matched employer-employee data with hours (IDA, BFL)

authors: Alex Xi He and Daniel le Maire
title: Managing Inequality: Manager-Specific Wage Premiums and Selection in the Managerial Labor Market
summary: Builds a manager-firm-worker matched dataset for the whole Danish population to estimate manager effects on wages. Manager-specific premiums are almost as important as firm premiums for between-firm wage inequality, are unrelated to productivity, and high-paying managers are more likely to be replaced after acquisitions.
data: Matched employer-employee data with manager identifiers (IDA, company registers)

authors: Benjamin Ly Serena
title: The Causal Effect of Scaling up Access to Psychotherapy
summary: A 2008 reform introduced 60 percent coverage of private psychotherapy for patients aged 18 to 37 with depression or anxiety. Using registers from 1995 to 2019, coverage reduces psychiatric hospital contacts, physical health care use and suicide attempts, leaves employment unchanged, and saves more in other health spending than it costs.

authors: Andrew E. Clark, Nicolai Kristensen and Niels Westergård-Nielsen
title: Job Satisfaction and Co-worker Wages: Status or Signal?
summary: Links survey measures of job satisfaction to register wages of all co-workers at the same establishment. Satisfaction is higher when co-workers earn more, the opposite of the usual income comparison result, which the authors interpret as co-worker pay signalling one's own future earnings; the effect is stronger for men and in the private sector.
data: Danish ECHP survey linked on PNR

authors: Mette Ejrnæs and Stefan Hochguertel
title: Is Business Failure Due to Lack of Effort? Empirical Evidence from a Large Administrative Sample
summary: Danish self-employed can voluntarily buy unemployment insurance, which creates a moral hazard test. Using a large administrative panel, insured entrepreneurs are more likely to close their businesses and enter unemployment, with effects that strengthen as the eligibility date approaches, consistent with reduced effort rather than selection alone.

authors: Paul Bingley, Lorenzo Cappellari and Niels Westergård-Nielsen
title: Unemployment Insurance, Wage Dynamics and Inequality Over the Life Cycle
summary: Models permanent and transitory wage dynamics over the life cycle for Danish men, allowing dynamics to differ by unemployment insurance membership. Insurance is associated with lower wage inequality and less persistence of shocks, and the paper quantifies how much of life-cycle wage inequality UI members avoid relative to non-members.
data: Register wages for a long panel of men (IDA, IND)

authors: Juanna Schrøter Joensen and Helena Skyt Nielsen
title: Mathematics and Gender: Heterogeneity in Causes and Consequences
summary: A pilot scheme in Danish high schools that let students combine advanced mathematics with chemistry increased advanced maths take-up, especially among girls. The induced maths qualification raised later earnings, with the gains concentrated among students who would otherwise have taken less maths and operating through higher education choices.
data: High school course registers and exam records

authors: Anders Frederiksen and Takao Kato
title: Human Capital and Career Success: Evidence from Linked Employer-Employee Data
summary: Uses complete Danish career histories to study who reaches top management, through internal promotion or external recruitment. Formal schooling and breadth of experience across occupations both help, they are complementary, and breadth acquired within the firm matters more than breadth acquired outside it, consistent with human capital theories of corporate leadership.
data: Matched employer-employee data with occupation codes (IDA)

authors: Sandra E. Black, Sanni Breining, David N. Figlio, Jonathan Guryan, Krzysztof Karbownik, Helena Skyt Nielsen, Jeffrey Roth and Marianne Simonsen
title: Sibling Spillovers
summary: Identifies spillovers within the family from having a disabled younger sibling using administrative data from both Denmark and Florida. Comparing first- and second-born children in families with three or more children, the second child, who spends more early childhood with the younger sibling, is differentially affected when the third child is disabled.
data: Medical Birth Register and patient registers for disability diagnoses

authors: Paul Bingley, Lorenzo Cappellari and Konstantinos Tatsiramos
title: Family, Community and Long-Term Socio-Economic Inequality: Evidence from Siblings and Youth Peers
summary: Decomposes sibling correlations in permanent earnings, education and unemployment for the Danish population into family and community components, allowing for life-cycle dynamics. Family is the dominant factor; community background shapes earnings and unemployment correlations early in working life but fades quickly.
data: Family and residence links (BEF, address histories)

authors: Steffen Andersen, Julie Marx, Kasper Meisner Nielsen and Lise Vesterlund
title: Gender Differences in Negotiation: Evidence from Real Estate Transactions
summary: Men appear to secure better prices than women in Danish real estate transactions, but the gap shrinks with better controls for property value and disappears in repeat-sales and inherited-property samples. The price differences reflect men and women demanding different properties, not differences in negotiation.
data: Owner characteristics and inheritance from registers

authors: Christian Dustmann, Mikkel Mertz and Anna Okatenko
title: Neighbourhood Gangs, Crime Spillovers and Teenage Motherhood
summary: Uses the random assignment of refugees to municipalities between 1986 and 1998. Gang crime in the assignment neighbourhood raises boys' probability of offending before 19 and girls' probability of teenage motherhood, with lasting consequences: more inactivity for men and lower earnings and more benefit claims for women at ages 19 to 28.

authors: Mikkel Aagaard Houmark, Victor Ronda, Esben Agerbo, Preben Bo Mortensen and Michael Rosholm
title: Genetic and Socioeconomic Achievement Gaps in Elementary School
summary: Shows that the achievement gap by polygenic score for educational attainment is as large as the gap by socioeconomic status and widens during elementary school, but only among low-SES children. Selection into neighbourhoods and schools explains part of the SES gap but none of the genetic gap, which instead relates to conscientiousness and the learning environment.
data: iPSYCH genotype data linked to registers

authors: Bent Jesper Christensen, Rasmus Lentz, Dale T. Mortensen, George R. Neumann and Axel Werwatz
title: On-the-Job Search and the Wage Distribution
summary: Estimates an on-the-job search model on the Danish Integrated Database for Labour Market Research, splitting each firm's separation rate into an exogenous part and a job-to-job part that falls with the firm's wage. Workers search less intensely the higher their wage, and the estimated model accounts for the gap between the distribution of wages earned and the distribution of wage offers.

authors: Anna Piil Damm
title: Ethnic Enclaves and Immigrant Labor Market Outcomes: Quasi-Experimental Evidence
summary: Uses the quasi-random dispersal of refugees across Danish municipalities between 1986 and 1998 to separate the effect of living in an ethnic enclave from self-selection. Larger enclaves raise refugee men's annual earnings without changing their employment rates, and the gains are larger where more co-nationals are employed, pointing to job information networks.

authors: Christian M. Dahl, Daniel le Maire and Jakob R. Munch
title: Wage Dispersion and Decentralization of Wage Bargaining
summary: Exploits the shift in Denmark during the 1990s from centralised to firm-level wage bargaining. Workers covered by firm-level bargaining earn a wage premium, returns to skills are higher, and wage dispersion is greater than under sector-level bargaining.
data: Matched employer-employee data with bargaining regime (IDA)

authors: Gustaf Bruze, Michael Svarer and Yoram Weiss
title: The Dynamics of Marriage and Divorce
summary: Estimates a dynamic model of marriage, divorce and remarriage with learning about match quality on long register histories of Danish cohorts. Spousal education is complementary in generating marital surplus, education stabilises marriages, education raises men's share of the surplus, and divorce costs are high both early and late in a marriage.
data: Marital histories from the population register (BEF)

authors: Paul Bingley and Alessandro Martinello
title: Measurement Error in Income and Schooling and the Bias of Linear Estimators
summary: Links survey reports of income and schooling for Danish respondents to the same variables in the registers. Measurement errors in survey income and schooling are correlated and non-classical, so standard corrections fail, and the paper quantifies the resulting bias in linear estimators such as returns to schooling.

authors: Pieter Gautier, Paul Muller, Bas van der Klaauw, Michael Rosholm and Michael Svarer
title: Estimating Equilibrium Effects of Job Search Assistance
summary: A randomised activation experiment in two Danish counties helped treated job seekers find work faster, but untreated job seekers in the same counties found work more slowly than in comparison counties. An equilibrium search model fitted to the data shows that these displacement effects make a large-scale rollout far less beneficial than the partial estimates suggest.

authors: Sanni Breining, Joseph Doyle, David N. Figlio, Krzysztof Karbownik and Jeffrey Roth
title: Birth Order and Delinquency: Evidence from Denmark and Florida
summary: In both Denmark and Florida, second-born boys are substantially more likely than their first-born brothers to be disciplined in school and to enter the criminal justice system. The evidence points to reduced parental time investment for later-born children, rather than differences in health at birth or neighbourhood, as the mechanism.
data: Family links and birth order (BEF, MFR)

authors: Paul Bingley, Petter Lundborg and Stéphanie Vincent Lyk-Jensen
title: The Opportunity Costs of Mandatory Military Service: Evidence from a Draft Lottery
summary: Uses the Danish draft lottery to estimate the effect of conscription on later outcomes. Military service delays education and labour market entry, and the paper quantifies the resulting losses in schooling and earnings for those who serve.

authors: Anne Ardila Brenøe and Ulf Zölitz
title: Exposure to More Female Peers Widens the Gender Gap in STEM Participation
summary: Exploits idiosyncratic variation in the share of female peers across cohorts within Danish high schools. A higher share of female peers lowers women's probability of enrolling in and graduating from STEM programmes and raises men's, widening the gender gap in STEM.
data: High school cohort and class registers

authors: Claudio Labanca and Dario Pozzoli
title: Constraints on Hours within the Firm
summary: Uses Danish linked employer-employee data with hours and tax-rate variation from the 2010 Danish tax reform. Employees in firms with tight constraints on working hours do not adjust their hours when their taxes change, while employees in more flexible firms respond both directly and through spillovers from their coworkers.

authors: Emma von Essen and Nina Smith
title: Network Connections and Board Seats: Are Female Networks Less Valuable?
summary: Uses Danish employer-employee data from 1995 to 2011 to study how professional networks affect first appointments to supervisory boards. Larger networks raise the chance of a board seat, more so for men, because men's networks connect them more often to larger and listed firms and to other men.
data: Matched employer-employee data (IDA) for network construction

authors: Anne Toft Hansen, Ulrik Hvidman and Hans Henrik Sievertsen
title: Grades and Employer Learning
summary: Uses a nationwide rescaling of Danish university grades to identify the return to GPA that is unrelated to ability. A reform-induced higher GPA raises earnings right after graduation, especially for graduates with fewer other signals, but the effect fades within a few years, consistent with employers learning quickly about productivity.

authors: Jonas Fluchtmann, Anita M. Glenny, Nikolaj A. Harmon and Jonas Maibom
title: Unemployed Job Search across People and over Time: Evidence from Applied-For Jobs
summary: Uses the logs of job applications made by Danish unemployment insurance recipients to document how the jobs people apply for differ across job seekers and change over an unemployment spell, and what these patterns imply for models of directed search.
data: Job application logs from the public employment service (Jobnet)

authors: Anne Ardila Brenøe, Serena Canaan, Nikolaj A. Harmon and Heather N. Royer
title: Is Parental Leave Costly for Firms and Coworkers?
summary: Compares small Danish firms where a female employee is about to give birth with similar firms without an impending birth. There is little evidence of negative effects on firm output or coworkers: most firms cover the absence by hiring temporary workers and raising other employees' hours, and only firms unable to reallocate work show losses.

authors: Mette Foged, Linea Hasager and Giovanni Peri
title: Comparing the Effects of Policies for the Labor Market Integration of Refugees
summary: Uses quasi-experimental variation from several Danish reforms to compare, in a common framework, the long-run employment and earnings effects of language training, active labour market programmes and benefit cuts for refugees, and ranks the policies by their effects and costs.

authors: Jacob Nielsen Arendt, Christian Dustmann and Hyejin Ku
title: Permanent Residency and Refugee Immigrants' Skill Investment
summary: A Danish reform tightened the employment and language requirements refugees must meet to obtain permanent residency. Rather than encouraging investment, it lowered overall employment and barely moved language proficiency, because refugees with weak pre-reform prospects reduced effort when the requirements looked out of reach.
data: Residence permit and permanent residency records

authors: Sadegh Eshaghnia, James J. Heckman and Rasmus Landersø
title: The Impact of the Level and Timing of Parental Resources on Child Development and Intergenerational Mobility
summary: Uses Danish registers covering parents' full income histories to separate the level of parents' lifetime resources from their timing during childhood. Lifetime resources matter far more than when income arrives, and conventional intergenerational elasticities based on short income windows give a misleading picture of mobility.

authors: Eskil Heinesen, Christian Hvid, Lars Kirkebøen, Edwin Leuven and Magne Mogstad
title: Instrumental Variables with Unordered Treatments: Theory and Evidence from Returns to Fields of Study
summary: Shows that the assumptions needed to identify returns to unordered treatments, such as fields of study, have testable implications, and characterises the bias when they fail. Using admission cut-offs and applicants' ranked choices in Denmark and Norway, payoffs to fields are strongly correlated across the two countries once fields violating the assumptions are dropped.

authors: Anders Frederiksen, Takao Kato and Nina Smith
title: Working Hours, Top Management Appointments, and Gender: Evidence from Linked Employer-Employee Data
summary: Links the Danish Labour Force Survey's detailed hours to register career histories. Long hours, hours relative to peers and nonstandard hours raise the odds of a top management appointment within the firm, and the gender gap in hours, driven mainly by supply-side factors, is a major contributor to the gender gap in reaching top management.
data: Danish Labour Force Survey linked on PNR

authors: Frederik Almar, Benjamin Friedrich, Ana Reynoso, Bastian Schulz and Rune Vejlin
title: Educational Ambition, Marital Sorting, and Inequality
summary: Classifies detailed Danish education programmes into ambition types by their graduates' starting wages and wage growth. Assortative matching by educational ambition has risen sharply even though sorting by conventional education levels looks flat, and the marriage market accounts for more than 40 percent of the rise in household income inequality since 1980.

authors: Michael Svarer, Michael Rosholm and Jakob Roland Munch
title: Rent Control and Unemployment Duration
summary: Uses Danish register data on unemployment spells and housing to study whether living in rent-controlled housing affects job finding. Unemployed workers in rent-controlled dwellings have lower exit rates from unemployment, consistent with rent control reducing geographic mobility.

authors: Paul Bingley and Gauthier Lanot
title: Public Pension Programmes and the Retirement of Married Couples in Denmark
summary: Estimates a dynamic discrete choice model of couples' joint retirement and saving on a 1 percent register sample of Danish couples, using the introduction and reforms of the early retirement programme (efterløn) for identification. Retirement responds asymmetrically for men and women to their own and their spouse's income flows.
data: 1 percent sample of the population registers

authors: Brian Krogh Graversen and Jan C. van Ours
title: How to Help Unemployed Find Jobs Quickly: Experimental Evidence from a Mandatory Activation Program
summary: A randomised experiment in two Danish counties assigned newly unemployed workers to an intensive activation programme with early job search courses, frequent meetings and mandatory activation. Treated workers found jobs substantially faster, with the threat of mandatory activation an important part of the effect.

authors: Nabanita Datta Gupta and Marianne Simonsen
title: Non-cognitive Child Outcomes and Universal High Quality Child Care
summary: Links the Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children to the registers to compare non-cognitive outcomes at age seven for children in universal preschool, family day care and home care at age three. Attending high-quality preschool does not harm non-cognitive outcomes relative to home care, while long hours in family day care are associated with worse outcomes for some groups.
data: Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children linked on PNR

authors: Daniel le Maire and Bertel Schjerning
title: Tax Bunching, Income Shifting and Self-Employment
summary: Self-employed Danes bunch sharply at the top tax kink, but much of the bunching reflects intertemporal shifting of income through retained earnings in the business rather than real changes in effort. Accounting for shifting implies a much smaller elasticity of real income.
data: Income tax records of the self-employed

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Jakob Roland Munch and Hans Jørgen Whitta-Jacobsen
title: Taxation and the Long Run Allocation of Labor: Theory and Danish Evidence
summary: Estimates a search model with non-linear taxation, in which workers keep looking for better-paid jobs, on employer-employee register data for all Danish workers and workplaces in 2004 to 2006. Danish taxes reduce total income by about 12 percent through the allocation of labour across jobs, and moving to low-tax OECD levels would recover four fifths of the loss.
data: Matched employer-employee data for the full population (IDA)

authors: Juanna Schrøter Joensen and Helena Skyt Nielsen
title: Spillovers in Education Choice
summary: Exploits the Danish high school pilot that made advanced mathematics cheaper to take for some cohorts. An older sibling's advanced maths choice raises the probability that the younger sibling also chooses advanced maths, with spillovers that depend on the siblings' gender composition.

authors: Maya Rossin-Slater and Miriam Wüst
title: Parental Responses to Child Support Obligations: Evidence from Administrative Data
summary: Uses discontinuities in the Danish child support schedule by fathers' income to estimate how higher obligations affect separated parents. The paper documents responses in fathers' income, subsequent family formation and the parents' living arrangements.

authors: Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Household Labor Supply and the Gains from Social Insurance
summary: Shows how the labour supply response of surviving spouses after a partner's death can serve as a sufficient statistic for the welfare value of survivors' insurance, and implements it with Danish administrative records on spousal deaths, earnings and transfers.

authors: Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Labor Supply and Optimization Frictions: Evidence from the Danish Student Labor Market
summary: Danish students lose part of their study grant when annual earnings exceed a threshold. Register data show bunching below the threshold that grows as students gain experience with the rule, so optimisation frictions hide a structural elasticity well above the observed response.

authors: N. Meltem Daysal, Michael Lovenheim, Nikolaj Siersbæk and David N. Wasser
title: Home Prices, Fertility, and Early-Life Health Outcomes
summary: For Danish homeowners aged 20 to 44, a 100,000 kroner rise in home prices raises the probability of giving birth by about 2.35 percent. Birth outcomes improve too, but mostly because of who gives birth, and there is no effect on children's health in the first five years.

authors: Marianne Simonsen, Lars Skipper, Niels Skipper and Anne Illemann Christensen
title: Spot Price Biases in Non-Linear Health Insurance Contracts
summary: The Danish prescription drug reimbursement scheme has coverage that rises with annual spending and resets each year. Consumers look forward-looking around the reset but react too strongly to current prices within the year, and liquidity constraints rather than plan literacy or cognitive decline explain the spot-price bias.

authors: Katrine Jakobsen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Identifying Behavioral Responses to Tax Reforms: New Insights and a New Approach
summary: Shows that standard estimates of taxable income elasticities from tax reforms are biased by mean reversion and diverging income trends across the distribution, and proposes an approach that exploits reform timing to separate behavioural responses from these trends, applied to Danish tax reforms.

authors: Mette Foged, Linea Hasager, Giovanni Peri, Jacob Nielsen Arendt and Iben Bolvig
title: Intergenerational Spillover Effects of Language Training for Refugees
summary: Follows the children of refugees affected by the 1999 Danish reform that improved language training. Children of treated parents achieve better educational outcomes, showing that the integration gains from language training carry over to the next generation.

authors: Sofie Cairo and Robert Mahlstedt
title: The Disparate Effects of Information Provision: A Field Experiment on the Work Incentives of Social Welfare
summary: A field experiment in Denmark informed welfare recipients about a minimum work requirement, either with personalised running counts of their hours or with generic rules. Personalised information raised employment among those below the required hours, while generic notices reduced labour supply among those at low near-term risk of sanctions.

authors: Hans Schytte Sigaard
title: Estimating Labor Supply Responses to Danish Tax Reforms
summary: Applies taxable income elasticity methods to register data on hours actually worked. The intensive-margin labour supply elasticity is about 0.08, close to the labour income and taxable income elasticities, and it comes from changes in contract hours, paid absence and switches between main and secondary jobs.

authors: Esteban García-Miralles and Jonathan M. Leganza
title: Joint Retirement of Couples: Evidence from Discontinuities in Denmark
summary: Uses age discontinuities in eligibility for Danish early retirement and public pensions to show that when one spouse becomes eligible and retires, the other spouse is substantially more likely to retire as well, quantifying spillovers that matter for evaluating retirement reforms.

authors: Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Jack Blundell
title: Income Effects and Labour Supply: Evidence from a Child Benefits Reform
summary: A 2011 Danish cap on child benefits cut payments to families with several young children and left smaller families unaffected. Mothers' labour supply rises substantially after the cut, mainly on the extensive margin, and sterilisation records are used to control for differences in preferences for more children.
data: Sterilisation records from the patient register

authors: Linea Hasager
title: Does Granting Refugee Status to Family-Reunified Women Improve Their Integration?
summary: Women who enter Denmark through family reunification usually hold permits that depend on staying married. Granting them independent refugee status improves their economic integration, raises divorce rates and lowers the risk of violence against them, consistent with reduced residency uncertainty and greater bargaining power.

authors: Thomas Høgholm Jørgensen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: The Division of Parental Leave: Empirical Evidence and Policy Design
summary: Uses sharp incentives in the Danish parental leave benefit system for about 190,000 births to estimate parents' willingness to pay for leave. Parents bunch at kinks and are willing to pay for a traditional split with little leave for fathers, and simulations show that earmarked leave works much better when combined with high replacement rates.

authors: Linea Hasager and Mia Jørgensen
title: Sick of Your Poor Neighborhood? Quasi-Experimental Evidence on Neighborhood Effects on Health
summary: Uses the quasi-random dispersal of refugees across Danish neighbourhoods from 1986 to 1998. Refugees placed in low-income neighbourhoods had a 12 percent higher risk of developing a lifestyle-related disease 8 to 15 years later, driven by neighbours and the local environment rather than health care access, ethnic networks or labour market outcomes.
